prompt: What makes `new Receipt().line(...).line(...)` possible?
hint: Look at the last line of `line`.

choices.text: `line` ends with `return this;`
choices.why: Right: the second call is made on the receipt the first one returned.

choices.text: A special chaining syntax enabled by the `fluent` keyword
choices.why: There is no such keyword; it is ordinary method calls on returned values.

choices.text: `Receipt` extending `StringBuilder`
choices.why: It extends nothing; it returns itself, as `StringBuilder` does.

choices.text: The `List<String>` field, which keeps the receipt alive between calls
choices.why: The list holds the lines; the chain works because of what `line` returns.

prompt: What total did the receipt print, in cents?
`card.setName("Ana").setNumber(1042)` failed with `void cannot be dereferenced`. What does the message mean?
hint: What did `setName` return?

choices.text: That `card` is `null`
choices.why: That would be a `NullPointerException` at run time; this is a compile error.

choices.text: That `setNumber` does not exist

choices.text: `setName` returned nothing

prompt: Why does the section advise against making every setter return `this`?
hint: Think of tools that read classes by their setters.

choices.text: Because returning `this` makes a copy of the object each time
choices.why: `return this` returns a reference to the same object; nothing is copied.

choices.text: `java.beans` recognises only `void` setters, and tools built on it would miss the rest
choices.why: Right: chaining suits a class meant to be configured in one go, not every bean.

choices.text: Because the compiler forbids a setter with a return value
choices.why: It allows it; `Receipt.line` is effectively one.

prompt: Why is `Loan`'s constructor `private`?
hint: What would a public one let a caller skip?

choices.text: So that `Loan` cannot be extended
choices.why: Preventing subclasses is `final`'s job; here the point is the checks.

choices.text: To force `build()`
choices.why: Right: every loan goes through `build()` and its checks, because the builder is the only way in.

choices.text: Because nested classes cannot call public constructors
choices.why: They can call any; private is chosen to close the other doors.

prompt: `Loan.of("Iracema").to("Ana").build()` set no period. What did it print?
hint: The builder's fields start at their defaults.

choices.text: `Iracema to Ana for 0 days`
choices.why: `days` starts at 21 in the builder, not at Java's default for an `int`.

choices.text: `Iracema to Ana for 21 days`
choices.why: Right: the default period, and no note.

choices.text: An `IllegalStateException`, since `days` was not set
choices.why: Only the member is required; the period has a default.

prompt: The third loan forgot `to(...)`. When was the mistake caught?
hint: The stack trace's first line after the message.

choices.text: At compile time, because `member` is required
choices.why: The compiler cannot see that a chain left out a call.

choices.text: When the loan was printed
choices.why: It was never printed; it was never built.

choices.text: In `build()`, before any `Loan` existed
choices.why: Right: `at Loan$Builder.build`, with a message naming the book.

choices.text: In `days(14)`, which checks the member first
choices.why: `days` only stores the number; every check is in `build()`.

prompt: Besides `Loan.class`, which class file did `ls Loan*.class` list?
hint: A nested class gets a file of its own.

choices.text: `Builder.class`
choices.why: The outer class's name is part of the file name.

choices.text: `Loan.Builder.class`
choices.why: The source writes a dot; the file name uses another character.

choices.text: `Loan$Builder.class`
choices.why: Right: outer name, a `$`, nested name.

choices.text: None: a nested class is compiled into `Loan.class`
choices.why: Every class, nested or not, gets its own class file.

prompt: According to the section's table, which situations call for a builder? Choose all that apply.
hint: A builder is a second class with every field written twice.

choices.text: Several optional fields with sensible defaults
choices.why: Yes: each is set by name, or left alone.

choices.text: Two required fields and nothing else
choices.why: No: a constructor or a record is simpler.

choices.text: Rules that involve more than one field at once
choices.why: Yes: `build()` sees every part together.

choices.text: Any class with a setter
choices.why: No: setters and builders answer different needs.

prompt: A colleague suggests replacing the builder with a public constructor `Loan(String book, String member, int days, String note)`. What does the section say goes wrong first?
hint: Read the caller's line, not the class.

choices.text: Every caller passes `21` and `""` for parts it does not care about, by position
choices.why: Right: and nothing says which number is the period.

choices.text: The loan becomes mutable
choices.why: A constructor with `final` fields keeps it immutable.

choices.text: The checks become impossible
choices.why: A constructor can check its arguments; the problem is the call sites.

choices.text: 31 October, as before the call

prompt: Why did the compiler say nothing about `title.toUpperCase();`?
hint: Is ignoring a result legal?

choices.text: Because `toUpperCase` changes the string in place
choices.why: It returned `IRACEMA` and `iracema` printed; nothing changed in place.

choices.text: Because warnings for ignored results are turned off by default in `javac`
choices.why: `javac` has no such check to turn on.

choices.text: Calling a method and discarding what it returns is legal Java
choices.why: Right: the language cannot tell a forgotten result from an unwanted one.

prompt: `BigDecimal total = BigDecimal.ZERO; for (...) { total.add(price); }` always ends at zero. What is wrong?
hint: `BigDecimal` sits in one row of the section's table.

choices.text: `BigDecimal.ZERO` is a constant and refuses `add`
choices.why: `add` works on it and returns a new value.

choices.text: `add` returns a new value and the loop throws it away
choices.why: Right: `total = total.add(price);`.

choices.text: The loop needs a `StringBuilder` to collect the sum
choices.why: `StringBuilder` builds text, not numbers.

choices.text: `price` is added before the loop starts
choices.why: Each iteration calls `add`; each result is lost.

prompt: `Receipt.line` changes the receipt and returns it. A colleague calls `receipt.line("fee", 150);` on a line of its own. Is the fee recorded?
hint: Which kind of chain is the receipt?

choices.text: Yes: `line` changed the receipt
choices.why: Right: ignoring `this` loses nothing, unlike ignoring a new object.

choices.text: No: like `plusDays`, the result has to be assigned
choices.why: That is the immutable kind; the receipt is the other.

choices.text: No: a chain must have at least two calls
choices.why: One call is a chain of one, and it runs normally.

prompt: What is a fluent interface?
hint: It is a design, not a keyword.

choices.text: An `interface` whose methods all have default bodies
choices.why: The word interface here means a class's surface, not the Java `interface`.

choices.text: Calls that chain into one expression
choices.why: Right: each method returns an object for the next call.

choices.text: A class whose methods take no parameters
choices.why: `line` and `days` take parameters and chain fine.
